questions.question: Explain how director becomes the creative force behind a film by analyzing the essay by Andrew Sarris. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• “Notes on Auteur theory” - Andrew Sarris - director- primary creative force behind a film -
  • Director as auteur (author) of a film - defends auteur theory in three premises - technical
  • competence (master the craft) - distinguishable personality (signature stylistic traits which
  • recurs in works) - interior meaning (the meaning/work generated from the tension between the
  • director’s personality and the material)
  • (CO4)

questions.solution_html:

  • establishing a shorthand that audiences understand instantly. Eg. the white hat represents
  • heroism, the black hat evil, and the saloon a realm of moral compromise - a genre's
  • iconography also indicates thematic values - this coding runs deeper than simply aesthetics to
  • include dialogue, music, and even casting.

questions.question: Discuss the socio-economic realities of the Great Depression depicted in the film. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• In Modern Times (1936), Charlie Chaplin portrays the Great Depression through satire
  • and symbolism that expose industrial dehumanization and social struggle - opening scene -
  • compares factory workers to sheep, showing how labourers were herded and controlled by the
  • system - the Tramp’s breakdown on the assembly line and his being swallowed by the machine
  • - Chaplin illustrates how industrial labour consumes both body and mind - Scenes of stealing
  • to survive, repeated unemployment, and being mis taken for a communist reflect the
  • desperation and political anxiety of the era - film ends with Charlie and the girl walking toward
  • an uncertain future - symbolizing hope, resilience, and human companionship - amid economic
  • despair.
  • (CO 1,2,3,4)

questions.question: Discuss the relationship between Michel and Patricia in Breathless. How does their dynamic reflect themes of alienation, freedom, and existential uncertainty? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In Breathless (1960), Jean-Luc Godard portrays Michel Poiccard and Patricia Franchini as
  • physically close but emotionally distant, reflecting modern alienation - Michel imitates
  • American gangster films, while Patricia’s emotional indecision and fragmented conversations
  • reveal disconnection and confusion - Dialogue often lacks coherence, mirroring disillusioned
  • mindset of the postwar generation - Michel’s amorality and criminal acts blur the line between
  • freedom and rebellion, while Patricia’s foreignness i n Paris represents a rootless sense of
  • liberty - their relationship becomes a temporary space of liberation, exposing the instability
  • and uncertainty of love and freedom in an existential world. (CO3)

questions.question: Discuss the concept of the auteur theory and its central role in the French New Wave movement. / [CO3] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Auteur Theory - coined by Andrew Sarris argues that the director is the primary creative
  • force behind a film, shaping it through personal style and thematic consistency - Auteur shows
  • technical competence, personal coherence, and a distinctive worldview across t heir works -
  • idea originated from the French New Wave of the 1950s and 1960s, which rebelled against
  • traditional storytelling and studio dominance - Critics from Cahiers du Cinéma promoted the
  • Politique des auteurs, emphasizing the director’s unique artistic vision over commercial
  • production - Director became viewed as the author of the film, expressing individuality and
  • creativity through cinematic form and narrative. (CO3)
  • (6 x 5 = 30)

questions.question: In what ways does Schatz’s concept of genre evolution from transparency to self-conscious formalism reflect shifts in cultural attitudes, and how do examples like The Searchers or The Band Wagon illustrate this progression in challenging traditional genre conventions? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Traditional film genres - straightforward storytelling - reflected dominant social ideologies –
  • met audience expectations - shift to self-conscious formalism - films more aware of their own
  • form and conventions - changing audience pleasure from passive enjoyment to recognizing
  • genre manipulation - John Ford’s The Searchers (1956) subverts the heroic Western - Ethan
  • Edwards as a racist, obsessive anti -hero - film’s moral ambiguity questions the myth of the
  • noble frontier and the clarity of traditional “genr es of order”- Vincente Minnelli’s The Band
  • Wagon (1953) parodies its own musical-romantic conventions, using self-awareness to satirize
  • the artifice of show business.
  • (CO2)
